subject: computer-science
title: Theory of Computation: Turing and FSMs
welcome_lead: Meet the abstract machines at the heart of computer science.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: Turing machines, finite state machines and what they can compute.
final_note: These models define the limits of what any computer can do.

concepts.def: An abstract machine with a finite set of states and transitions triggered by inputs; it has no memory beyond knowing its current state.
A graph showing an FSM's states as circles and its transitions as labelled arrows, with designated start and accepting states.
An abstract model of computation with an infinite tape, a read/write head, a state register and a transition rule table.
A Turing machine that can simulate any other Turing machine by reading that machine's description from its own tape.
The proven result that no general algorithm can decide, for every program and input pair, whether the program will eventually halt.
The study of which problems can be solved by algorithms at all; some well-defined problems, like the halting problem, are non-computable.

walkthroughs.body_html: Alan Turing's 1936 machine has an infinite tape, a read/write head and a finite control. Despite its simplicity, it can compute anything any modern computer can — the Church-Turing thesis formalises this idea.

An FSM has finitely many states and transitions but no memory beyond the current state. They model traffic lights, vending machines and lexers — they cannot count arbitrarily but they are fast and easy to verify.

FSMs recognise regular languages. Push-down automata (FSM + stack) recognise context-free languages. Turing machines recognise everything computable — but cannot answer every question (see the halting problem).

mcqs.q: A finite state machine consists of:
options: A finite set of states with transitions between them triggered by inputs
An infinite tape and a read/write head
Unlimited random access memory
A database of all possible answers

mcqs.q: A Turing machine includes which components?
options: An infinite tape, a read/write head, a state register and transition rules
A monitor, mouse and keyboard
A finite tape that cannot be written to
Two CPUs sharing one cache
No general algorithm can decide whether every program halts on every input
All programs eventually stop
Computers cannot run loops
Every problem can be solved with enough memory

mcqs.q: A universal Turing machine is special because it can:
options: Simulate any other Turing machine from a description on its tape
Solve the halting problem
Run without any transition rules
Operate faster than light

mcqs.q: Does the halting problem mean we can never tell whether any program halts?
options: Yes - the halting problem says all programs run forever.
Yes - it is impossible to know if any program will ever finish.
No - many individual programs can easily be proven to halt or loop; the theorem says no single GENERAL algorithm works for all programs and inputs.
Yes - a Turing machine is another name for the Bombe.

mcqs.q: Can a finite state machine count an unbounded number of items, such as matching nested brackets?
options: No - an FSM's only memory is its current state, so with finitely many states it cannot track unbounded counts; that needs a stack or more powerful model.
Yes - adding more arrows gives an FSM unlimited memory.
Yes - an FSM can remember any amount of information in its transitions.
Yes - a Turing machine is another name for the Bombe.

mcqs.q: Is a Turing machine a physical computer that was built in the 1930s?
options: Yes - Turing machines were the first commercially sold computers.
Yes - the halting problem says all programs run forever.
Yes - a Turing machine is another name for the Bombe.
No - it is an abstract mathematical model used to define what is computable; its infinite tape means it cannot be fully built, only simulated.
